text: A blob container is where objects actually live inside a storage account — the Azure equivalent of the bucket concept you already learned in object storage, with an S3 bucket as its closest parallel. Blob names can contain slashes that make the Azure portal display something that looks like folders, but underneath, the namespace stays completely flat, exactly the same object-storage idea you already know.

Create a container with az storage container create, naming the storage account and the container itself. Every blob you put inside that container sits in one of three access tiers, and the tradeoff those tiers make is always the same shape: a lower storage cost in exchange for a higher retrieval cost, and sometimes a real retrieval delay measured in hours instead of milliseconds.

Hot costs the most to store but effectively nothing extra to read, with no delay — the right fit for data you touch constantly. Cool costs less to store than Hot, a little more to retrieve, and fits data accessed infrequently but still needed quickly, typically kept for thirty days or more. Archive is the cheapest tier by far, but the data is genuinely offline: reading it back means submitting a rehydration request first, and that can take hours, not milliseconds.

Walk through a real example: nightly database backups. Keep the first seven days in Hot, because if something breaks you want the most recent backup available instantly with zero delay. Move day eight through ninety into Cool — still fast enough, but far cheaper than paying Hot prices for a backup you're now unlikely to restore. Move anything older than ninety days, kept only to satisfy a compliance mandate, into Archive, where an hours-long wait is a completely acceptable tradeoff for the savings.

Upload a blob directly into Cool or Archive by setting --tier on az storage blob upload, right at upload time. Next lesson takes this same blob storage and compares it directly against Azure Files and Managed Disks, mapping all three of Azure's real storage products onto the object, file, and block storage concepts you already learned in the prior course.
